en: They fought him face-to-face
And waged a mighty battle.
Firing guns and loosing arrows,
They cut down all who faced them,
Waging strife beyond mortal bounds.
When a khan grows obstinate, he dies;
All who grapple in battle die.
In such a place heroes die,
And many men die together;
Great rulers die and khans die,
And all who fight die.
When the whole world gathers,
When two sides clash,
When two heroes fight,
The guiltless multitude suffers;
There is a great tumult of battle cries—
Such is the fury of holy war.
Yielding to no one who approached,
His prowess was extraordinary,
His heroism beyond compare;
He cut down all he faced,
Slaughtering as he advanced.
Yielding to no multitude,
Sarybai, son of a monster,
Grew far fiercer
Than he had been before.
The three heroes surrounded him,
And when they leveled their keen spears
And struck him from every side,
He did not so much as blink or frown;
He never bowed his head before conflict.
They could not overpower him in combat;
They roared but could not break his strength.
When they grappled, their weapons could not pierce him;
Against that wrathful, calamitous infidel,
Even blazing saxaul wood could raise no ember.
The whole world could not overcome him;
At anyone he faced, Sarybai
Kept thrusting his spear.
A savage struggle, a great calamity—
Sarybai kept creating it.
Like a wolf, Sarybai
Kept tearing apart all he encountered.
A fierce struggle, a mighty battle—
Sarybai kept waging it.
Though the three heroes surrounded him,
He did not flinch when struck with clubs,
He did not groan when cut by swords,
He did not stir when pierced by spears.
Conflict could not subdue him;
When they contended with that swine,
They could not find the slightest means against him.
Then Sarybai
Was seized by still fiercer wrath
And did not stand watching without fighting.
He was no mere nail as before;
His fury mounted and possessed him.
Brave Seytek, born of a lion,
Turned the gray kulan steed’s head;
Kuyaly’s men and Külchoro
Had taken up this cause
And now sought the way forward.
When Sarybai, son of a monster,
Unleashed his wrath,
The wide world grew narrow.
The mighty, broad-shouldered man
Grew old beneath his trials.
Under Sarybai’s venom,
Under the calamity of his wrath,
All the people despaired.
The savage lion ranged unchecked,
And all who faced him were slain.
He hunted, encircled, and cut them down;
The people endured terrible hardship.
He greatly multiplied their wounds
And showed them endless suffering.
He made his guests spend the night
And forced them to recount long tales;
He brought many forms of destruction
And shot men down from above,
Making their days one unbroken torment.
When the people spread over the summer pastures beneath the blue road,
When summertime arrived,
When snowdrop blossoms bloomed
And nightingales perched in the willows,
When living souls spared from death
Swarmed like tiny blue ticks,
He poured out his fury more fiercely.
Seizing anyone left behind,
He tore apart their ribs.
Heroes died and khans died;
All who confronted him died.
The eyes of the skillful were pierced,
And under this infidel’s venom,
All he met were beheaded.
Army upon army surged together;
A great many people were slain.
He unleashed a raging, disastrous conflict—
Such was his lionlike ferocity.
All who survived death saw
His smoke set the heavens ablaze,
Tormenting my soul;
He mangled all he encountered,
Gnawed apart all he met,
And grew fat from drinking blood.
He slaughtered livestock down to the black camels,
And filled his sword’s scabbard with blood.
Until destruction had run its course,
A dense and tangled conflict raged.
“I am the hero Külchoro;
Many tens of thousands of warriors came,
Yet this swine Sarybai
Attacked my caravan from the hills,
And still I have not taken my revenge.”
“I am the hero Seytek;
If fate has come, let me die.
This vile swine has run mad;
Let me test myself against him.
Unwavering, I shall bring disaster upon him;
If my hand can reach him, for my honor
I shall take my long-awaited revenge.
Against this pestilent swine
I shall ride out in single combat.
Enraged against the infidel,
To break his mighty strength,
I shall certainly go alone.
I shall strike hard with my spear;
Let me clash with him and see.
Ten thousand troops have slipped from his hand;
Let me see the extent of his strength.
I shall rain shots upon him
And leave such a mark
For the ruined nation to remember.
He is Sarybai and I am Seytek;
We shall clash with battle cries,
Unleash calamity upon each other,
Struggle without sparing our lives,
And fight to the finish;
I shall make a wondrous slaughter.
Not sparing my thread-thin life,
I shall fight him to the end.
I have longed to meet him face-to-face
And kindle another battle;
My early word has grown late,
And my two eyes have become four with waiting—
To thrust my spear with all my might,
To stand against him face-to-face,
To learn the fate written on my brow,
And see it all fulfilled;
If God should put me to the test,
To surrender my precious life;
To observe and discover
His courage and heroism.
If he is a champion and a hero,
If the fiend Sarybai is a valiant man,
If such is the destiny of a brave lion,
And if I am the hero Seytek,
I shall call every champion who comes against me
To account for it all.
I shall not flee from the wrathful infidel,
But meet him in battle.
If the Creator grants me honor,
I shall perform a wondrous deed,
Beat down his long-held fury,
And stand face-to-face with him
To unleash a great commotion.
Not a single thread-thin life shall remain;
We shall slaughter one another to the last.
I have composed my account;
I have sought the road to Sarybai.
We shall ride out and joust in single combat,
Until a great uproar reaches its height.
Prepared for that very thing,
We shall unleash a battle.
We shall advance in force and see,
For we ourselves burn with desire.
We bow to the will of God;
We long to enter single combat
And strike him down.
We stand consumed by that desire.
Against this Sarybai on the plain,
Who gives no quarter to anyone with a jaw,
And yields to no rider on a bareback horse,
Whose strength cannot be matched in wrestling,
Whom we cannot overcome in combat,
All our saplings have been blown down,
All our scouts have been exhausted,
And we stand driven from our course.
We are guarding the place where we shall die,
Standing as though about to depart.
At Kara-Buura in Chatkal,
Along the winding Kyrgyz road,
Grime rained down upon our heads,
And all four kinds of livestock scattered;
A fierce battle began.
He slaughtered everyone without exception.
He chased the deer until they became cattle;
He cut all of us down.
Would a prince’s descendant,
Whose heart feared combat,
The only son of a noble house,
Be thrown into confusion by a hero
And possess a spirit like mine?
My opponent is Sarybai;
I am riding out against the enemy,
And shall reach him and strike with my spear.
If I do not fight this slave,
May I sink unborn into oblivion;
May I die rather than live.
This swine seems to have run mad;
Let me test myself against him.
When Sarybai pours out his venom,
Has he no bullet aimed at his brow,
No ancestral bullet
Among the heroic Kyrgyz people?
Did we break through the turmoil and clear a road,
Attacking a people trapped without escape?
Did we leave him trembling in torment,
With his spear driven into the earth,
That he should wreak such slaughter
And create this battle?
Did we steal away his piebald mare,
Or scatter the white-fleeced wealth
Of that dishonored swine?
Did we drive off his gray mare,
As though scattering all his gathered possessions?
Calling ourselves his lord and khan,
Did we disgrace him in public
And scatter all he had amassed?
Did we ravage his outskirts and drive him away?
Did we taste the flesh
Of that maddened swine?
Did we seize all his possessions?
Did the swine’s suffering overwhelm him,
Or did we leave him looking behind?
Did Kuyaly break faith and become embroiled,
His thoughts disturbed and brooding,
Hiding himself as something precious?
Did I steal the plunder away,
Or seize his camel stallion?
Unless we destroyed the crops
Of his people spread across the land,
Unless we killed warriors and slaughtered nations
And became foolish bloodthirsty men,
Why did he inflict such tyranny and shame?
He made us cry out like a nation rich in pacers,
Quenching the fires we had lit
And sending souls fleeing in droves;
He seized and cruelly humiliated the innocent.
God sees his tyranny,
Yet he showed no regard for high station.
He wounded those bound by oath.
He brought evil upon my people,
Broke my back again and again,
And threw my nation into confusion.
